candidate.source_to_sink_explanation: The worker POST first queries existing site bindings and rejects conflicts. It then independently upserts on organization_id,external_key, including the new site_id. Concurrent requests for the same new external key can both observe no existing row and then upsert different site IDs; the later write wins without either request receiving WORKER_SITE_TRANSFER_REQUIRED.
supporting_source_evidence: The conflict lookup and upsert are separate database statements.
The unique key serializes the final upsert but does not preserve the site observed by the precheck.
candidate.title: Worker site-transfer protection is vulnerable to a check-then-upsert race
candidate.violated_security_invariant: A worker already associated with one site must not be reassigned to another site without the explicit transfer procedure.

candidate.attacker: An authenticated organization owner issuing parallel MCP-token requests.
candidate.concrete_impact: A tenant can mint more active MCP bearer capabilities than the admission policy allows, increasing credential sprawl and bypassing the intended per-site issuance bound.
counterevidence: Issued tokens are random, hashed at rest, time-bounded, tenant-bound, and checked for site/organization consistency during authentication.
The race does not grant cross-tenant scope.
candidate.recommended_remediation: Issue tokens through an atomic database function that takes a per-site advisory lock or locks a quota row, counts active unexpired tokens, inserts only when below the limit, and returns the new row. Apply request-rate admission as defense in depth.
candidate.source_to_sink_explanation: The token route counts active tokens, checks the maximum in application code, and then inserts a new token in a separate statement. Parallel requests can all observe a count below the limit and each receive a distinct valid plaintext token.
supporting_source_evidence: The count and insert are independent PostgREST operations.
The database has an index for counting active tokens but no constraint or issuance function enforcing the cap.
candidate.title: MCP active-token quota can be exceeded by concurrent issuance
candidate.violated_security_invariant: A site may have no more than the configured maximum number of active, unexpired MCP bearer capabilities.

candidate.attacker: An authenticated user issuing concurrent first-use requests.
candidate.concrete_impact: Tenant data, workers, workpacks, and MCP tokens can be split across duplicate workspace roots, creating inconsistent authorization scope and operational records.
counterevidence: All resulting organizations remain owned by the same authenticated user.
This does not directly cross a tenant boundary.
candidate.recommended_remediation: Define the intended cardinality and enforce it with unique constraints. Use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT or a transactional provisioning RPC, then return the canonical rows.
candidate.source_to_sink_explanation: ensureWorkspaceContext selects the first organization owned by the user and inserts one if absent, then separately selects and inserts a site. Neither organizations.owner_id nor sites(organization_id,name) is unique. Concurrent first-use requests can therefore create multiple organizations or duplicate same-name sites and return different workspace contexts.
supporting_source_evidence: Provisioning uses independent select-then-insert statements.
The schema has no uniqueness constraint for owner_id or organization/site name.
candidate.title: Workspace provisioning can create duplicate tenant roots under concurrency
candidate.violated_security_invariant: A user should be provisioned into one canonical organization and one canonical site for a given organization and site name.

candidate.attacker: Any authenticated PostgREST user if authenticated-role privileges exist on dispatch_logs.
candidate.concrete_impact: Any authenticated user could read, alter, or delete every null-organization dispatch row, exposing recipient contact information or corrupting dispatch history.

candidate.source_to_sink_explanation: dispatch_logs.organization_id is nullable. Its FOR ALL RLS policy explicitly authorizes every row whose organization_id is null, without checking auth.uid(). Such rows may contain target_contact, payload, provider state, workflow IDs, and failure details.
supporting_source_evidence: Both USING and WITH CHECK accept organization_id IS NULL.
The table schema permits null organization IDs and stores contact and payload fields.
candidate.title: Nullable dispatch-log tenant IDs create a globally shared authenticated RLS scope
candidate.violated_security_invariant: Dispatch targets, contacts, payloads, and provider results must always belong to a specific authorized organization.

candidate.attacker: An anonymous or authenticated PostgREST caller if inherited deployment grants permit access.
candidate.concrete_impact: Under permissive inherited grants, a caller could read or modify every legacy document and query-log row because the database has no row-level authorization predicate.

candidate.recommended_remediation: If unused, revoke anon/authenticated privileges and migrate or remove the tables through an approved process. If retained, add explicit ownership, enable and force RLS, define least-privilege policies, and add regression tests for anonymous and cross-tenant denial.
candidate.source_to_sink_explanation: The initial migration creates documents and query_logs but never enables RLS, revokes public-schema privileges, or adds tenant ownership columns. No later migration hardens them. The application distributes a browser Supabase URL and anon key, so any inherited PostgREST privileges would reach unscoped tables.
supporting_source_evidence: All later migrations were reviewed and none enables RLS or revokes privileges for these tables.
Neither table contains organization_id, owner_id, or another tenant-binding column.
candidate.title: Legacy documents and query_logs tables have no repository-enforced RLS boundary
candidate.violated_security_invariant: Document contents and user query logs must be explicitly tenant-scoped or server-only.

candidate.attacker: Unauthenticated caller rotating sessionId or workerId values in Share acknowledgement requests.
candidate.concrete_impact: A caller can raise acknowledgement database work from the intended per-capability limit to the coarser pre-body limit, increasing service-role lookups and verification work.
counterevidence: Pre-body distributed admission caps requests at 60 per minute and eight concurrent body reads.
Bodies are limited to 16 KiB.
Known recipients must provide the complete stored phone number or email before a confirmation is written.
candidate.recommended_remediation: Retain the coarse caller identity in the ACK key or enforce both caller and capability quotas. Do not let the worker identifier replace the stable caller dimension.
candidate.source_to_sink: POST first applies a stable pre-body quota and concurrency lease, but subsequently keys the 20-request acknowledgement limiter only by caller-controlled sessionId and workerId. Rotating either value bypasses that fine-grained quota before service-role session lookup and contact verification.
supporting_source_evidence: The pre-body namespace uses the default client identity.
The later share-session-ack namespace replaces it with `${sessionId}:${workerId || "anonymous"}`.
candidate.title: Share ACK fine-grained quota can be partitioned after coarse admission
candidate.violated_security_invariant: The operation-specific acknowledgement quota must remain bound to a stable caller identity.
